newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call eases as market get grip on instruments.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call eases as market get grip on instruments.

text.p: Dutch call rates eased slightly on Friday, as market players got to grips with the new monetary policy instruments introduced last Friday.
Call money was changing hands at between 3.19 and 3.25 percent, down from 3.18/31 bid/ask on Thursday.

"It seems market players are getting used to the new instruments. They realise they shouldn't save too much under their cash reserve (with the central bank) because that isn't rewarded," one dealer said.
Since last Friday, market players had been very careful not to end up with a debit balance at the end of the day.
Any negative gap would be automatically filled at an interest rate of 4.5 percent at the end of the day.
"But there's quite some money being offered now, notably by major banks," another dealer said.
He said the state itself was also not in need of funds, as month-end tax payments were coming in today.
Dealers said this morning's allocation of 3.56 billion guilder under a new, seven-day, special advances pact had contributed to ease overnight rates as well.
"The allocation was quite ample," one said.
With its 3.84 billion guilders, the previous pact had offered more money.
But that pact had been bigger than usual as the central bank had adapted its size to give market players some more leeway while finding its feet with the new money market instruments, he said.
Dealers said they had not noticed any trade in Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs) this morning.
"The Agent has lowered his (indicative) prices over the last few days, while money market rates have gone up," one dealer said. "You can see they don't need money at the moment."
DTCs maturing at the end of June were set at 3.10 percent, those end-August at 3.12 percent and those end-December 3.19 percent.
Dealers said this morning's announcement by the Finance Ministry's Agency that, as of July, it would increase transparency in its DTC issues, did not have any impact on the market at the moment.
"But notably foreign players wanting to get into short paper will be pleased with it," one said.
The guilder fractionally strengthened against the mark, quoting 112.503 per 100 marks versus 112.525 on Thursday.
